units.title: The Table
units.blurb: The place setting, the courses of a tasting menu, service styles and the pass.

topics.title: Plate Composition
topics.short: Choose the plate, then build with color, height and texture; leave clear space; odd numbers of pieces look natural; keep the rim clean.
topics.trouble: Beginners fill every inch of the plate, or stack everything into a tall tower that falls over at the table.

topics.title: Sauce Work and Garnish
topics.short: Pools, dots, swooshes and spoon drags; every garnish should be edible and belong to the dish.
topics.trouble: Cooks pour the sauce over the crispy skin they worked to make crisp.

topics.title: The Place Setting: Utensils, Glasses and Plates
topics.short: Forks on the left, knives and spoons on the right, used from the outside in; glasses above the knives; the bread plate at upper left; dessert utensils above the plate.
topics.trouble: Diners and new servers mix up the bread plate and the glasses: solids on the left, liquids on the right.

topics.title: The Courses of a Tasting Menu
topics.short: Many small courses in an order that builds: a small bite from the chef, lighter to richer, savory to sweet, often with cheese before dessert and small sweets at the end.
topics.trouble: New cooks serve full portions on a tasting menu, and guests are full by course four.

topics.title: Service Styles: French, Russian, American and Family
topics.short: Plated (American) service comes from the kitchen on the plate; Russian service is served from platters at the table; French (guéridon) service finishes dishes on a cart beside the table; family style passes platters.
topics.trouble: Learners mix up French and Russian service, which in history meant something different from what they mean in restaurants today.

topics.title: The Pass: Firing and Calling Tickets
topics.short: The expediter calls each order, the stations answer "heard", courses are fired so they finish together, and every plate is checked before it leaves.
topics.trouble: Cooks start each dish when they see it instead of when it is fired, so a table's plates finish minutes apart.
